report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, which President Trump called “Liberation Day,” the U.S. announced two tiers of new tariffs: a 10% baseline tariff on most imported goods, effective April 5, and higher “reciprocal” tariffs for selected trading partners, scheduled to start April 9. The higher rates replaced the 10% baseline for those partners; they were not added on top of it. (whitehouse.gov)
| Trading partner | Rate announced April 2 |
|---|---:|
| Lesotho | 50% |
| Cambodia | 49% |
| Vietnam | 46% |
| China | 34% |
| Taiwan | 32% |
| India | 26% |
| South Korea | 25% |
| Japan | 24% |
| European Union | 20% |
These are selected rates from the executive order’s original schedule. Canada and Mexico were excluded from this tariff package and remained under separate tariff rules. Some products were also exempt, including pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and steel and aluminum already subject to separate tariffs. (whitehouse.gov)
The announced rates changed quickly: China’s rate was raised before the original 34% took effect, and most other higher rates were paused starting April 10, leaving the 10% baseline in place for most trading partners. (usitc.gov)

quotes.text: Such rates of duty shall apply with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on April 5, 2025
all articles imported into the customs territory of the United States shall be, consistent with law, subject to an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 percent

pages.quote_reason: The quotes back the 10% ad valorem duty on imported articles and the April 5, 2025 effective date, but they say all articles rather than most, and they never describe the tariff as a baseline.
pages.page_reason: The page states that all articles imported into the customs territory of the United States are subject to an additional 10 percent ad valorem duty for goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT on April 5, 2025, with exceptions for certain in-transit goods and provisions for Annex I countries, which supports the claim that the 10% baseline applied to most imports effective April 5.

quotes.text: The additional ad valorem duty on all imports from all trading partners shall start at 10 percent and shortly thereafter, the additional ad valorem duty shall increase for trading partners enumerated in Annex I to this order at the rates set forth in Annex I to this order.

all articles from trading partners enumerated in Annex I to this order imported into the customs territory of the United States shall be, consistent with law, subject to the country-specific ad valorem rates of duty specified in Annex I to this order.

pages.quote_reason: The first quote says the duty starts at 10 percent on all trading partners and then increases for Annex I partners, which implies the higher rates build on the 10% baseline rather than replacing it, while the second quote only says the country-specific rates apply without saying whether they replace the 10%.
pages.page_reason: The page says the additional duty starts at 10 percent and then 'shall increase' for Annex I partners to the rates in Annex I, which suggests a higher rate but never explicitly states that the higher rates replaced the 10% baseline or were not stacked on it.

quotes.text: With respect to articles from Canada, I have imposed additional duties on certain goods to address a national emergency resulting from the flow of illicit drugs across our northern border

With respect to articles from Mexico, I have imposed additional duties on certain goods to address a national emergency resulting from the flow of illicit drugs and illegal migration across our southern border

Any ad valorem rate of duty on articles imported from Canada or Mexico under the terms of this order shall not apply in addition to the ad valorem rate of duty specified by the existing orders described in subsection (d) of this section.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes show that Canada and Mexico were subject to separate additional-duty orders tied to illicit drugs and migration, which backs the separate tariff rules, but nothing in them mentions an April 2 tariff package or says Canada and Mexico were excluded from it.
pages.page_reason: The page states that Canada and Mexico goods are subject to separate border-emergency duties under Executive Orders 14193/14194 and related amendments, and that Annex I country rates and subsection (e) interact with those orders, but it does not explicitly say Canada and Mexico were excluded from the April 2 package; it instead indicates that their articles are subject to ad valorem rates under this order (e.g., 12 percent if the orders terminate, and non-USMCA goods face the rates in this order's framework), so the exclusion claim is not clearly supported.
